disease.name: Migraine
disease.icd_10_code: G43 (Migraine); G43.0 (Migraine without aura); G43.1 (Migraine with aura); G43.3 (Complicated migraine); G43.7 (Chronic migraine); G43.8 (Other migraine); G43.9 (Migraine unspecified)

overview.description: Migraine is a complex, chronic, disabling neurological disorder characterised by recurrent attacks of moderate to severe, typically unilateral, throbbing or pulsating headache lasting 4 to 72 hours, frequently accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and extreme sensitivity to light (photophobia) and sound (phonophobia). Approximately 25-30% of migraineurs experience an aura — transient, reversible neurological symptoms (most commonly visual zigzag lines, scotomas, or sensory disturbances) preceding or accompanying the headache. Migraine is the third most prevalent disease globally and the second leading cause of disability worldwide, being the leading cause of disability in people under 50 years of age.
overview.affected_organ: Brain and central nervous system (trigeminovascular system); also affects cranial blood vessels, meninges, and the brainstem
overview.prevalence: Affects approximately 1 billion people worldwide; prevalence ~14-15% globally; ~12% of the US population; ~15% in Europe; ~8-9% in India (Hingee et al. estimate 150-200 million in India).
overview.age_group: Can begin at any age; peak onset 15-55 years; most common in adults 25-55 years; affects all ages including children. Childhood migraine prevalence 7-10%.
overview.sex_ratio: Women are 2-3 times more likely to have migraine than men after puberty (hormonal influence of oestrogen). Before puberty, equal in boys and girls.
overview.disability_burden: Leading cause of years lived with disability (YLD) in under-50s globally. WHO ranks migraine among the top 10 most disabling conditions worldwide.

migraine_phases.description: A complete migraine attack can progress through up to 4 distinct phases — though not all patients experience all phases in every attack.

phases.timing: Hours to 2 days BEFORE headache onset
symptoms: Food cravings — particularly for sweet or salty foods; chocolate
Cognitive difficulty — trouble concentrating, memory problems
Increased sensitivity to light and sound before headache begins
phases.clinical_importance: Recognizing prodrome allows early treatment and trigger avoidance; yawning is highly predictive

phases.timing: 5-60 minutes, immediately before or during the early headache phase
phases.prevalence: ~25-30% of migraineurs; not present in migraine without aura

aura_types.type: Visual Aura (most common — 90% of all auras)
aura_types.features: Positive phenomena: scintillating scotoma (bright zigzag arc of light — 'fortification spectra'); flashing lights (photopsia). Negative phenomena: scotoma (area of vision loss/dimming). Usually starts small, slowly expands over 20-30 minutes, moves across visual field. Binocular (both eyes affected — from occipital cortex).
Pins and needles or numbness that slowly spreads ('marching' paresthesia) from hand to face or face to hand — 'cheiro-oral march'. Unilateral. Slow spread over 20-30 minutes distinguishes from TIA.
Difficulty finding words (dysphasia), slurred speech, or confusion. Must distinguish from TIA/stroke — aura develops gradually over >5 minutes; TIA typically abrupt.
Weakness or hemiplegia — requires specific diagnosis of Hemiplegic Migraine. Can be severely disabling; triptans and ergots CONTRAINDICATED.
Dysarthria, vertigo, tinnitus, diplopia, bilateral sensory symptoms, ataxia, or decreased consciousness. Triptans relatively contraindicated.

phases.cortical_spreading_depression: Aura is caused by cortical spreading depression (CSD) — a slow wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation followed by sustained inhibition, spreading across the cortex at 2-5 mm/min. This generates the expanding/moving quality of aura symptoms.

features: Unilateral in 60-70% (may be bilateral in 30-40%, especially children)
Pulsating or throbbing quality — often described as 'heartbeat in the head'
Moderate to severe intensity (prevents normal activity)
Worsened by routine physical activity (walking, climbing stairs)

Cutaneous allodynia — light touch feels painful (skin hypersensitivity from central sensitization — develops 60-90 minutes into attack, signals established central sensitization; triptans less effective after this point)

phases.timing: Up to 48 hours AFTER headache resolves
symptoms: Light and sound sensitivity persisting mildly
phases.clinical_importance: Postdrome significantly extends migraine-related disability beyond headache resolution

types.name: Migraine Without Aura (Common Migraine)
types.description: The most common form — accounting for ~75% of migraine cases. Attacks fulfil the core ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria (unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, worsened by activity, with nausea/vomiting or photophobia+phonophobia) WITHOUT preceding or accompanying neurological aura symptoms.
types.common_in: Adults 25-55 years; women 3x more than men
types.diagnostic_criteria: ≥5 attacks; 4-72 hours; ≥2 of: unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, worsened by activity; ≥1 of: nausea/vomiting, photophobia AND phonophobia

types.name: Migraine With Aura (Classic Migraine)
types.description: Migraine preceded or accompanied by transient, reversible focal neurological aura symptoms — most commonly visual (zigzag scintillating scotoma, fortification spectra). Aura typically lasts 5-60 minutes; each symptom gradually develops over ≥5 minutes; no single symptom lasts >60 minutes. Headache follows within 60 minutes of aura (or occurs simultaneously in some cases).
types.common_in: 25-30% of migraineurs; associated with slightly increased stroke risk in women who smoke or use oestrogen-containing OCP

types.name: Chronic Migraine
types.description: Headache occurring on ≥15 days per month for >3 months, with ≥8 days/month meeting migraine criteria (or responding to triptan/ergot). A major disabling condition — affects ~2% of the population. Often develops from episodic migraine through progression (transformation), frequently driven by medication overuse (MOH).
types.common_in: Adults; women more than men; patients with frequent episodic migraine on analgesics
types.management: Preventive medication essential; withdrawal from overused medications; CGRP mAbs highly effective

types.name: Hemiplegic Migraine
types.description: Rare, severe form of migraine with aura that includes fully reversible motor weakness (hemiplegia or hemiparesis). Can be familial (FHM — autosomal dominant mutations in CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A genes) or sporadic. Motor weakness can last from hours to days and can be severely disabling. Must differentiate from stroke.
types.common_in: Rare — affects <0.01% of population; can occur in children
types.contraindications: Triptans, ergotamines, and beta-blockers are CONTRAINDICATED
types.management: Preventive therapy (flunarizine, verapamil, acetazolamide, lamotrigine); naproxen or IV ketorolac for acute attacks; specialist management

types.name: Vestibular Migraine
types.description: Migraine variant characterized by recurrent vestibular episodes (vertigo, dizziness, imbalance) lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours, occurring in patients with current or history of migraine, with migraine features during ≥50% of vestibular episodes. Second most common cause of recurrent vertigo. Often misdiagnosed as Ménière's disease or BPPV.
types.common_in: Adults; women more than men; 1-3% of population; 10% of migraine patients
types.management: Migraine preventives (propranolol, topiramate, amitriptyline, venlafaxine); vestibular rehabilitation; avoid triggers

types.name: Retinal Migraine
types.description: Repeated attacks of monocular visual disturbance (visual loss, scintillations, or scotoma) affecting ONE EYE ONLY (monocular — from retinal ischaemia) associated with migraine headache. Unlike typical aura (binocular from occipital cortex), retinal migraine is monocular and potentially vision-threatening.
types.warning: Retinal migraine is a DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION — other causes of monocular visual loss (retinal artery occlusion, carotid embolism, optic neuritis) must be urgently excluded

types.name: Menstrual Migraine
types.description: Migraine attacks occurring exclusively or predominantly around menstruation. Pure menstrual migraine (PMM): attacks ONLY on days -2 to +3 of menstruation. Menstrually-related migraine (MRM): majority of attacks around menstruation but also at other times. Triggered by oestrogen withdrawal preceding menstruation. Typically more severe, longer, and more resistant to treatment.
types.common_in: 50-70% of female migraineurs have menstruation as a trigger; PMM in ~10%
types.management: Hormonal management (oestrogen patches/gel in oestrogen-withdrawal phase); frovatriptan or naratriptan mini-prophylaxis; triptans for acute attacks

types.name: Brainstem Aura Migraine (Basilar-Type Migraine)
types.description: Migraine with aura symptoms clearly originating from the brainstem (dysarthria, vertigo, tinnitus, hypacusis, diplopia, bilateral sensory symptoms, decreased consciousness) WITHOUT motor weakness. Previously called 'basilar artery migraine' — this term is now discouraged as basilar artery involvement not always demonstrated.
types.common_in: More common in adolescents and young women
types.contraindications: Triptans relatively contraindicated (caution — risk of basilar artery vasoconstriction); ergots contraindicated

types.name: Status Migrainosus
types.description: A debilitating migraine attack lasting >72 hours (beyond the typical 4-72 hour window) despite treatment. Severe disability; may lead to dehydration, medication overuse, and emergency department presentation. Requires parenteral treatment.
types.management: IV antiemetics (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide), IV DHE, IV ketorolac, IV dexamethasone, IV fluids; hospital admission may be needed

types.name: Migraine with Brainstem Aura in Children (Periodic Syndromes)
types.description: Childhood migraine equivalents — paroxysmal conditions that evolve into migraine or are strongly associated with migraine: Cyclical vomiting syndrome (recurrent episodes of intense vomiting), Abdominal migraine (recurrent midline abdominal pain with nausea), Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood, Benign paroxysmal torticollis.
types.management: Cyproheptadine, pizotifen, or propranolol for prevention; supportive care for acute episodes

severity_levels.name: Mild Migraine
severity_levels.description: Mild to moderate headache that does not significantly prevent daily activities
severity_levels.functional_impact: Able to function; reduced efficiency; may complete tasks with effort
severity_levels.midas_grade: Grade I — little or no disability (MIDAS score 0-5)
severity_levels.management: Simple analgesics as first-line (paracetamol, ibuprofen, aspirin); anti-emetics; trigger avoidance; keep migraine diary

severity_levels.name: Moderate Migraine
severity_levels.description: Moderate headache with significant impact on daily function
severity_levels.functional_impact: Normal activity partially restricted; productivity significantly reduced
severity_levels.management: Triptans as first-line acute treatment; consider preventive therapy if ≥4 attacks/month; combine triptan + NSAID if needed

severity_levels.name: Severe Episodic Migraine
severity_levels.description: Severe headache with complete or near-complete functional incapacitation during attacks
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unable to perform normal activities; bed rest required
severity_levels.midas_grade: Grade III — moderate disability (MIDAS 11-20) or Grade IV — severe (MIDAS >21)
severity_levels.management: Triptans first-line; preventive therapy strongly indicated; consider CGRP mAbs if standard preventives fail; acute parenteral treatment (IM sumatriptan, rectal diclofenac)

severity_levels.name: Chronic Migraine
severity_levels.description: ≥15 headache days per month (≥8 meeting migraine criteria) for >3 months — often with medication overuse headache
severity_levels.functional_impact: Severe disability; profound impact on employment, relationships, social life, and mental health
severity_levels.management: Mandatory preventive therapy; withdrawal from overused medications under medical supervision; botulinum toxin type A; anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies; multidisciplinary pain management; psychological support

pathophysiology.overview: Migraine is a complex neurovascular disorder with a strong genetic basis. The fundamental mechanism involves abnormal activation of the trigeminovascular system — pain-sensing neurons innervating the meninges and cerebral blood vessels — leading to neurogenic inflammation, vasodilation, and sensitization of both peripheral and central pain pathways.

key_mechanisms.description: A slow (2-5 mm/min) wave of sustained neuronal and glial depolarisation followed by prolonged inhibition, spreading across the cortex. Responsible for migraine aura. CSD activates meningeal nociceptors and triggers the trigeminovascular cascade.

The trigeminal nerve (CN V) innervates the pain-sensitive meninges and large cerebral vessels. When activated, its terminals release CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide), substance P, and neurokinin A — causing neurogenic inflammation (mast cell degranulation, plasma protein extravasation) and vasodilation. CGRP is the central mediator of migraine pain and the target of the newest migraine-specific treatments (gepants, CGRP mAbs, lasmiditan).

After 1-2 hours into a migraine attack, central sensitization develops — second-order trigeminal neurons in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis (TNC) and third-order thalamic neurons become sensitized. This explains cutaneous allodynia (light touch feels painful — a diagnostic marker of established central sensitization) and why triptans lose effectiveness once allodynia develops.

CGRP is markedly elevated during migraine attacks and returns to baseline after successful triptan treatment. CGRP causes: marked vasodilation, neurogenic inflammation, activation of pain receptors, and mast cell degranulation. Blocking CGRP or its receptor (gepants, CGRP mAbs) effectively treats and prevents migraine.

The hypothalamus — the 'migraine generator' — activates early in the prodrome phase (before headache or aura). Explains prodrome symptoms (yawning, fatigue, food cravings, photophobia before headache), circadian patterns of migraine attacks, and why CGRP mAbs targeting the pituitary gland area are effective.

Serotonin levels fall during migraine attacks. Triptans (selective 5-HT1B/1D agonists) mimic serotonin action on the trigeminovascular system — causing vasoconstriction of meningeal vessels, inhibiting CGRP release, and blocking pain signal transmission at the TNC.

genetic_factors: Migraine has one of the highest heritabilities among common complex diseases — 40-65%
First-degree relatives of migraineurs have 4-fold higher risk of migraine with aura; 2-fold higher risk of migraine without aura
>100 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with migraine risk identified through GWAS
Key genetic pathways: glutamatergic neurotransmission, pain signalling, ion channel regulation, vascular function

Rare monogenic migraine forms: Familial Hemiplegic Migraine types 1-3 (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A mutations — ion channel genes); CADASIL (NOTCH3 mutation — cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy — associated with migraine with aura)
MTHFR C677T polymorphism — associated with migraine with aura and mildly increased stroke risk

triggers: Menstruation — oestrogen withdrawal before menstruation triggers 50-70% of female migraineurs
Ovulation — mid-cycle oestrogen surge can trigger attacks in some women
Oral contraceptive pill — oestrogen-containing pills; pill-free week particularly problematic
Pregnancy — first trimester may worsen; 2nd and 3rd trimester often improve
Menopause — transitional phase worsens; postmenopause often improves
Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) — can worsen migraine with aura
Alcohol — particularly red wine (histamine, tyramine, sulfites) and beer; most potent dietary trigger
Caffeine — both excess and caffeine withdrawal (missing morning coffee) trigger attacks
Aged and fermented cheeses — tyramine content (cheddar, blue cheese, camembert, stilton)
Processed and cured meats — nitrates and nitrites (salami, bacon, hot dogs, ham)
Monosodium glutamate (MSG) — Chinese restaurant syndrome; also hidden in many packaged foods
Artificial sweeteners — aspartame (NutraSweet) particularly implicated
Chocolate — phenylethylamine (PEA) and caffeine content
Citrus fruits — biogenic amines in some individuals
Skipping meals — hypoglycaemia triggers attacks in many migraineurs
Dehydration — one of the most consistent and avoidable triggers
Too much sleep (weekend migraine — oversleeping at weekends)
Too little sleep or sleep deprivation
Disrupted sleep schedule — jet lag, shift work
Sleep apnoea — morning headaches and migraine worsening
Insomnia — both a trigger and consequence of migraine
Bright or flickering lights — sunlight, fluorescent lights, computer screens, strobe lights
Strong odors — perfumes, cigarette smoke, paint fumes, chemicals
Loud noises — concerts, machinery, traffic
Weather changes — barometric pressure changes (falling pressure most common)
Strong winds — Foehn wind, Chinook wind, khamsin
Psychological stress — both during stress and 'let-down' after stress ('weekend migraine')
Anxiety — independent comorbidity and trigger
Emotional upset or excitement
Relaxation after stress — the post-stress drop is a classic migraine trigger
Intense physical exertion — heavy lifting, strenuous exercise
Neck and shoulder muscle tension — cervicogenic component
Poor posture — prolonged desk work, forward head posture
Sexual activity (in rare cases — can trigger exertional migraine)
Head injury or concussion — post-traumatic migraine
Extended screen time — digital eye strain
Medication overuse headache (MOH) — paradoxical worsening from using acute analgesics, triptans, or opioids on ≥10-15 days per month
Nitrates (nitroglycerin, isosorbide) — trigger migraine within hours through NO pathway
Oral contraceptive pills — oestrogen fluctuation
Vasodilators
Histamine H2 blockers (cimetidine)

primary_symptoms.name: Severe Unilateral Headache (Hemicrania)
primary_symptoms.description: The defining symptom — moderate to severe throbbing or pulsating headache, typically affecting one side of the head (though may be bilateral in 30-40%, especially in children and postdrome). Classically involves the frontotemporal or periorbital region. Described as 'heartbeat in the head' or 'pounding'. Distinguishes from tension headache by its unilateral nature, pulsating quality, and incapacitating severity.
primary_symptoms.onset: Gradual build over 30 minutes to several hours; peak intensity within 1-2 hours of onset

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea and Vomiting
primary_symptoms.description: Nausea occurs in approximately 80% and vomiting in 50% of migraine patients. Gastric stasis occurs during migraine attacks (gastroparesis), delaying absorption of oral medications — explains why oral analgesics often work poorly once nausea is established. Vomiting may provide temporary relief of headache in some patients.
primary_symptoms.onset: Concurrent with or following headache onset
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Gastric stasis impairs oral drug absorption — consider faster routes (IM, nasal spray, dissolving tablet, rectal suppository)

primary_symptoms.name: Photophobia (Light Sensitivity)
primary_symptoms.description: Extreme sensitivity to light — even normal indoor lighting causes severe pain, eye discomfort, and worsening of headache. Patients retreat to dark rooms. Present in >80% of migraine attacks. Even after headache resolves, mild photophobia often persists into the postdrome. Driven by thalamic activation during migraine.
primary_symptoms.onset: During headache phase; sometimes begins in prodrome

primary_symptoms.name: Phonophobia (Sound Sensitivity)
primary_symptoms.description: Extreme sensitivity to sounds — even normal ambient noise causes severe pain and distress. Patients require silence. Present in >80% of migraine attacks. Patients often describe sounds as 'too loud' and 'piercing'. Contributes significantly to the social and occupational disability of migraine.

primary_symptoms.name: Aura Symptoms (in Migraine with Aura)
primary_symptoms.description: Transient, fully reversible focal neurological symptoms developing gradually over ≥5 minutes and lasting 5-60 minutes, preceding or accompanying headache. Visual aura (most common): scintillating scotoma — a bright, crescent-shaped arc of zigzag, flickering light that slowly expands across the visual field over 20-30 minutes, leaving a blank area in its wake. Sensory aura: tingling/numbness spreading from fingers to face. Speech aura: word-finding difficulty or slurred speech.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Moderate (aura itself); reassuring when patient recognizes them as migraine
primary_symptoms.onset: 5-60 minutes before or with headache; each symptom develops over ≥5 minutes

primary_symptoms.name: Osmophobia and Sensory Hypersensitivity
primary_symptoms.description: Smell sensitivity (osmophobia) — strong odors such as perfumes, food smells, cigarette smoke, cleaning products, or flowers trigger or worsen headache. Present in ~40% of attacks. Osmophobia is actually more specific to migraine than to tension headache. Allodynia — normally painless stimuli (brushing hair, wearing glasses, wearing tight clothing) feel painful due to central sensitization.
primary_symptoms.onset: During headache phase; osmophobia may precede headache

secondary_symptoms: Neck pain and stiffness — present in up to 75% of migraineurs; sometimes misattributed to meningitis
Cognitive impairment — 'brain fog': difficulty thinking, concentrating, memory lapses
Dizziness and vertigo — especially in vestibular migraine
Facial pain and pressure — pain spreading to jaw, eye, or cheek
Nasal congestion and rhinorrhoea — autonomic changes mimic sinusitis (often misdiagnosed as 'sinus headache')
Scalp tenderness and allodynia — painful to touch or comb hair
Visual disturbances (even without formal aura) — blurry vision, difficulty focusing
Tearing (lacrimation) and red eye — autonomic features
Abdominal pain (especially in children — abdominal migraine)
warning_signs_of_attack: Excessive yawning — highly specific prodrome symptom; start medication early
Sudden intense 'thunderclap' headache — worst headache of life — NOT migraine until subarachnoid haemorrhage excluded (EMERGENCY)
Visual aura symptoms gradually spreading (normal) versus sudden complete vision loss in one eye (retinal emergency)
Aura lasting >60 minutes or headache not following aura — possible TIA or stroke
New neurological symptoms with headache: weakness, speech difficulty, confusion (may indicate stroke)
Fever with severe headache and neck stiffness — possible meningitis (EMERGENCY)
Headache worsening over days/weeks progressively — not typical migraine pattern — brain tumour, subdural haematoma must be excluded
symptoms_in_children: Headache is often bilateral (frontal) in children — unlike adult unilateral pattern
Attacks are shorter — 1-72 hours (diagnostic minimum reduced to 1 hour in children)
GI symptoms often prominent — nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain (abdominal migraine equivalent)
Cyclical vomiting syndrome — recurrent episodes of intense vomiting without headache; migraine equivalent
Abdominal migraine — recurrent midline abdominal pain without headache; later evolves into typical migraine
Children may be pale, listless, and prefer lying in dark quiet room
Motion sickness very common in children who later develop migraine
School performance affected during prodrome, attack, and postdrome

flags: Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats)
Neurological symptoms or signs (weakness, sensory loss, altered consciousness)
New onset headache or different from usual headache pattern
Onset sudden (thunderclap — worst headache of life — SAH until proven otherwise)
Onset after 50 years of age (new headache)
Progressive headache worsening over weeks to months
Positional headache (worse lying down or standing — raised/low ICP)
Precipitated by Valsalva, cough, exertion, or sexual activity
Painful eye with autonomic features (periorbital) — cluster headache or glaucoma
Papilloedema or pulsatile tinnitus (raised intracranial pressure)

diagnosis.important_note: Migraine is a clinical diagnosis based on history and examination — there is NO specific diagnostic test or biomarker. Investigations are ordered only to EXCLUDE secondary causes (red flags). Normal investigations do not diagnose migraine — the diagnosis rests on fulfilling ICHD-3 criteria.

ichd3_criteria_without_aura.A: At least 5 attacks fulfilling criteria B-D
ichd3_criteria_without_aura.B: Headache attacks lasting 4-72 hours (untreated or unsuccessfully treated); in children 1-72 hours
ichd3_criteria_without_aura.C: Headache has at least 2 of: (1) Unilateral location; (2) Pulsating quality; (3) Moderate or severe pain intensity; (4) Aggravation by or causing avoidance of routine physical activity
ichd3_criteria_without_aura.D: During headache, at least 1 of: (1) Nausea and/or vomiting; (2) Photophobia AND phonophobia
ichd3_criteria_without_aura.E: Not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis

ichd3_criteria_with_aura.A: At least 2 attacks fulfilling B and C
ichd3_criteria_with_aura.B: One or more of: (1) Visual aura; (2) Sensory aura; (3) Speech and/or language aura; (4) Motor aura; (5) Brainstem aura; (6) Retinal aura
ichd3_criteria_with_aura.C: At least 3 of: (1) At least one aura symptom spreads gradually over ≥5 min; (2) Two or more aura symptoms occur in succession; (3) Each aura symptom lasts 5-60 min; (4) At least one aura symptom is unilateral; (5) At least one aura symptom is positive; (6) Aura accompanied or followed by headache within 60 min
ichd3_criteria_with_aura.D: Not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis, and TIA excluded

medical_history: Headache onset, frequency, duration, and progression over time
Headache characteristics: location (unilateral vs bilateral), quality (pulsating, pressure, stabbing), severity (VAS 1-10)
Associated symptoms: aura (describe in detail — visual, sensory, speech), nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia
Aggravating factors: physical activity, movement, light, sound
Relieving factors: dark room, sleep, cold/hot compress, vomiting
Trigger factors: menstrual cycle, foods, alcohol, sleep, stress, weather
Family history of migraine (strong genetic component)
Medication history: current acute and preventive treatments; medication frequency (screen for MOH)
Headache diary review: days per month, pattern, medication use days
Impact on daily life: MIDAS questionnaire (Migraine Disability Assessment Score); HIT-6 (Headache Impact Test)
Psychiatric comorbidities: depression and anxiety (bidirectional relationship with migraine)
Hormonal history in women: menstrual relationship, OCP use, pregnancy plans, menopause status
physical_examination: Blood pressure measurement — hypertension can cause headaches; baseline for antihypertensive preventive use
General appearance: pain behaviour, pallor, photophobia posturing (eyes covered)
Neurological examination: mental status, cranial nerves (II-XII), motor (power, reflexes), sensory, cerebellar (coordination), gait — should be NORMAL in primary migraine
Fundoscopy: papilloedema (raised ICP) — mandatory if atypical features
Neck examination: meningism (neck stiffness, Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs) — exclude meningitis
Temporal artery palpation: tenderness, reduced pulse, nodularity (giant cell arteritis in >50 years)
Head and face examination: sinuses (tenderness), temporomandibular joint (TMJ), teeth, scalp
Cardiovascular examination: aortic stenosis murmur, cardiac arrhythmias (relevant if considering triptans)
Pericranial muscle tenderness: suboccipital, trapezius, temporalis muscles (cervicogenic contribution)

diagnostic_tests.description: 5-question validated questionnaire measuring migraine-related disability over 3 months. Scores days lost or significantly impaired at work, household tasks, and leisure activities. Essential for treatment decisions.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Quantify migraine-related disability; guide treatment escalation; monitor response to preventive therapy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Grade I: 0-5 (little/no disability); Grade II: 6-10 (mild); Grade III: 11-20 (moderate); Grade IV: ≥21 (severe disability)

diagnostic_tests.description: 6-question validated questionnaire assessing the impact of headaches on normal daily activities, social activities, work/school, and psychological wellbeing.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess headache impact; screen for migraine; monitor preventive treatment response
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Score <49: no/little impact; 50-55: some; 56-59: substantial; ≥60: severe impact

diagnostic_tests.description: Daily record of headache days, intensity, duration, associated symptoms, triggers, medications used, and their effectiveness. Essential for establishing diagnosis, identifying patterns, monitoring frequency, screening for MOH, and evaluating treatment response.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Establish diagnosis; identify triggers and patterns; screen for medication overuse (MOH); guide and monitor treatment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: ≥8 migraine days/month with ≥15 headache days/month = chronic migraine; analgesic use ≥10-15 days/month = medication overuse

diagnostic_tests.test_name: MRI Brain (with and without gadolinium contrast)
diagnostic_tests.description: Gold standard for brain imaging. NOT routinely required for typical migraine fulfilling diagnostic criteria. Indicated for: atypical or changing headache pattern, first or worst headache, neurological signs or symptoms between attacks, red flag features, or failed response to multiple treatments.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude secondary causes: brain tumour, vascular malformations (AVM, dural AVF), Chiari malformation, cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT), subdural haematoma, encephalitis, demyelinating disease
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal MRI does NOT diagnose migraine — it excludes other causes. Migraine-specific MRI changes: white matter hyperintensities (non-specific; more common in migraine with aura)

diagnostic_tests.description: Faster than MRI but less sensitive for most pathologies. First-line in acute thunderclap headache emergency (better for acute subarachnoid haemorrhage in first 12 hours) or when MRI is unavailable.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Acute headache emergencies: subarachnoid haemorrhage, intracranial haemorrhage, acute hydrocephalus. CT angiography for vascular causes.
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal CT in first 6 hours after thunderclap headache: sensitivity ~98% for SAH. If CT negative and clinical suspicion high — proceed to LP.

diagnostic_tests.description: Imaging of cerebral and cervical blood vessels without invasive catheter angiography. Indicated when vascular pathology suspected: cerebral artery dissection (neck trauma, young stroke), arteriovenous malformation, giant cell arteritis (MR temporal artery), basilar artery abnormality.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect cerebral artery dissection, AVM, intracranial aneurysm, GCA (temporal artery); exclude CADASIL
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: In hemiplegic or basilar migraine: CTA/MRA to exclude vascular cause

diagnostic_tests.description: Essential when subarachnoid haemorrhage suspected but CT is negative (CT negative in 2% of SAH cases at 6 hours). CSF shows xanthochromia (yellow discoloration from bilirubin) 2-4 hours after SAH, persisting for 2 weeks. Also indicated for suspected meningitis or raised ICP.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage (when CT negative); exclude meningitis (bacterial, viral, fungal); diagnose raised ICP (pseudotumour cerebri); diagnose low CSF pressure headache
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Xanthochromia on spectrophotometry is the gold standard for SAH detection when CT is negative

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Blood Tests — ESR, CRP, Full Blood Count
diagnostic_tests.description: Not diagnostic for migraine. ESR and CRP are essential to screen for giant cell arteritis (GCA) in any new headache in patients over 50 — a headache emergency (risk of blindness). FBC to detect anaemia (exacerbates headache), thrombocytosis, or infection.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for GCA (new headache >50 years); screen for anaemia, infection, and systemic causes of headache
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: ESR >50 mm/hr with new unilateral temporal headache in >50 years: strongly consider GCA — urgent temporal artery biopsy and high-dose steroids

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Blood Tests — Metabolic Panel (Glucose, Electrolytes, Renal Function, LFTs, TFTs)
diagnostic_tests.description: Baseline workup for newly diagnosed migraine and before starting preventive medications. Thyroid dysfunction (both hypo- and hyperthyroidism) can cause headaches. Required before prescribing topiramate (renal stones risk), valproate (LFTs), or amitriptyline (cardiac).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Baseline before preventive medication; screen for metabolic causes of headache (hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbances, thyroid disease)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: TSH: thyroid dysfunction can cause headaches; glucose: hypoglycaemia is a trigger; LFTs and renal function: baseline for valproate and topiramate

diagnostic_tests.description: Recommended before prescribing tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline) for migraine prevention — to exclude baseline prolonged QTc, AV block, or bundle branch block. Also relevant before triptans in patients with cardiovascular risk.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Baseline cardiac assessment before amitriptyline; screen for arrhythmias and conduction defects; screen for contraindications to triptans in high-risk patients
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: QTc >450ms (men) or >470ms (women): caution with amitriptyline and triptans

diagnostic_tests.description: In patients with visual aura: to distinguish migraine aura from: ophthalmic migraine (retinal migraine — monocular), visual hallucinations from other causes, and genuine retinal pathology. Fundoscopy and visual field testing may be needed. Intraocular pressure for glaucoma (acute angle-closure glaucoma causes severe headache with painful red eye).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Distinguish retinal migraine from retinal pathology; exclude glaucoma (acute angle-closure); assess papilloedema
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal fundoscopy does NOT exclude migraine; papilloedema requires urgent investigation for raised ICP

medicines.note: Migraine medications are divided into ACUTE (abortive — taken during an attack to stop it) and PREVENTIVE (prophylactic — taken daily to reduce attack frequency). All medications should be prescribed by a licensed physician or neurologist. Self-medication can lead to medication overuse headache (MOH) — a paradoxical worsening from overuse of acute medications.

medication_overuse_headache_warning.definition: Headache occurring on ≥15 days/month in a patient using analgesics/triptans on ≥10-15 days/month for >3 months
medication_overuse_headache_warning.medications_causing_MOH: Opioids and combination analgesics (>10 days/month); triptans, ergots, NSAIDs (>10-15 days/month)
medication_overuse_headache_warning.management: Withdrawal of overused medication (under medical supervision); preventive therapy; often headache worsens transiently during withdrawal before improving
medication_overuse_headache_warning.prevention_rule: Use acute migraine medications on NO MORE than 10-15 days per month

categories.category_name: Simple Analgesics and NSAIDs — Acute Treatment (First-Line for Mild-Moderate)
categories.purpose: First-line acute treatment for mild to moderate migraine attacks. Must be taken early in the attack before nausea onset for best absorption. Anti-emetics should be combined.
categories.note: Take as soon as attack begins — do not wait for headache to intensify. Avoid on >10-15 days/month to prevent MOH.

medicines.name: Ibuprofen
medicines.dosage: 400-800 mg at onset; may repeat 400 mg after 4-6 hours; max 2400 mg/day
medicines.use_case: First-line NSAID for mild-moderate migraine; most evidence from RCTs; highly effective when taken early
medicines.tip: Soluble/liquid ibuprofen absorbs faster than standard tablets — better during migraine gastric stasis

medicines.name: Aspirin (Acetylsalicylic Acid)
medicines.dosage: 900-1000 mg at attack onset; effervescent form absorbs faster
medicines.use_case: Effective for mild-moderate migraine; effervescent formulation particularly useful due to faster absorption despite gastric stasis; aspirin 900mg + metoclopramide 10mg = highly effective combination
side_effects: Avoid in children under 16 (Reye's syndrome risk)

medicines.name: Naproxen Sodium
medicines.dosage: 500-1000 mg at onset; may repeat 500 mg after 6-8 hours; max 1250 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Longer-acting NSAID; effective for migraine; useful for attacks that tend to last longer; also used for menstrual migraine prevention (NSAID mini-prophylaxis)

medicines.name: Diclofenac Potassium
medicines.dosage: 50-100 mg at onset; diclofenac potassium sachet dissolves in water — fastest oral NSAID absorption
medicines.use_case: Rapid-onset NSAID for migraine; sachets give fastest GI absorption even during gastric stasis; approved for migraine specifically in some markets
medicines.note: Diclofenac potassium sachet formulation has fastest absorption among oral NSAIDs

medicines.name: Paracetamol / Acetaminophen
medicines.dosage: 1000 mg (2 × 500mg tablets) at onset; may repeat every 4-6 hours; max 4000 mg/day
medicines.use_case: Mild migraine; pregnancy (safest analgesic); patients with NSAID contraindications; children
side_effects: Minimal side effects at therapeutic dose
medicines.note: Evidence for paracetamol alone in migraine is modest; more effective combined with caffeine or aspirin

medicines.name: Aspirin + Paracetamol + Caffeine (Combination)
medicines.dosage: 2 tablets (each: aspirin 250mg + paracetamol 250mg + caffeine 65mg) at onset; max 2 doses per day
medicines.use_case: First-line OTC combination for mild-moderate migraine; caffeine enhances analgesic absorption and potentiates pain relief; NNT=5 for being pain-free at 2 hours
side_effects: Caffeine dependency with frequent use — can cause caffeine withdrawal headache
Max 2 days per week to avoid MOH

categories.purpose: Gold standard acute treatment for moderate-severe migraine. Triptans are selective serotonin (5-HT1B/1D) agonists causing: (1) Vasoconstriction of dilated meningeal blood vessels; (2) Inhibition of CGRP and other neuropeptide release from trigeminal terminals; (3) Inhibition of pain signal transmission in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis. Most effective when taken EARLY in the attack before central sensitization/allodynia is established.
categories.key_principle: Take at headache onset — do not wait for headache to reach full intensity. Less effective if taken during aura. Best absorbed as wafer, nasal spray, or injection if nausea/vomiting present.
contraindications: Ischaemic heart disease / coronary artery disease

medicines.name: Sumatriptan
medicines.form: Tablet (50mg, 100mg), Nasal spray (10mg, 20mg), Subcutaneous autoinjector (6mg), Rectal suppository (25mg)
medicines.dosage: Oral: 50-100mg at onset; nasal spray: 10-20mg; SC injection: 6mg SC; repeat after 2 hours if partial or no response; max 2 doses per attack; max 200mg/day oral
medicines.use_case: MOST WIDELY USED triptan worldwide; gold standard comparator in triptan trials; SC injection most effective (90-minute pain relief in 70%); nasal spray useful with nausea; injection fastest onset (10-15 min)
side_effects: Triptan sensations — chest tightness, pressure, throat/jaw heaviness (common, non-cardiac, benign)
medicines.evidence: NNT for pain freedom at 2h: SC injection ~2.5; 100mg oral ~5.0; nasal spray ~5.5

medicines.name: Zolmitriptan
medicines.form: Tablet (2.5mg, 5mg), Oral dissolving tablet (ODT), Nasal spray (2.5mg, 5mg)
medicines.dosage: 2.5-5mg at onset; may repeat after 2 hours; max 10mg/day
medicines.use_case: Very well-tolerated triptan; ODT useful with nausea (dissolves on tongue without water); nasal spray fast-acting; also active against photophobia and phonophobia

medicines.name: Rizatriptan
medicines.dosage: 5-10mg at onset; may repeat after 2 hours; max 20mg/day; use 5mg with propranolol (increases rizatriptan levels)
medicines.use_case: Fast-acting triptan; ODT wafer dissolves without water; 2h pain relief in 67-77%; good for rapid-onset attacks
medicines.note: Dose reduce to 5mg if taking propranolol (propranolol is a CYP inhibitor that doubles rizatriptan levels)

medicines.name: Eletriptan
medicines.dosage: 20-40mg at onset; may repeat after 2 hours; max 80mg/day
medicines.use_case: One of most effective triptans in NNT analyses; 2h pain freedom in 40-65%; good for attacks that do not respond to sumatriptan; lipophilic — penetrates CNS well

medicines.name: Almotriptan
medicines.dosage: 6.25-12.5mg at onset; may repeat after 2 hours; max 25mg/day
medicines.use_case: Favorable tolerability profile; low recurrence rate; approved for adolescents 12-17 years
side_effects: One of lowest side effect profiles among triptans

medicines.name: Naratriptan
medicines.dosage: 1-2.5mg at onset; may repeat after 4 hours; max 5mg/day
medicines.use_case: Slow onset but longer duration — lowest recurrence rate among triptans; used for mini-prophylaxis of menstrual migraine (1mg twice daily for 5 days from day -2 to +3 of menstruation); good for migraines that often recur
side_effects: Fewest side effects of all triptans
medicines.unique_use: Perimenstrual mini-prophylaxis to prevent menstrual migraine attacks

medicines.name: Frovatriptan
medicines.dosage: 2.5mg at onset; may repeat after 2 hours; max 7.5mg/day
medicines.use_case: Longest half-life of all triptans (~26 hours) — lowest recurrence rate; MINI-PROPHYLAXIS for menstrual migraine (2.5mg twice daily for 6 days perimenstrually — 2 days before expected menstruation); not fastest-acting
medicines.unique_use: Perimenstrual mini-prophylaxis — gold standard short-term hormonal migraine prevention

categories.category_name: CGRP Receptor Antagonists (Gepants) — Acute and Preventive Treatment
categories.purpose: The newest class of small-molecule migraine-specific drugs. Block the CGRP receptor (or CGRP ligand) without causing vasoconstriction — no cardiovascular contraindications (key advantage over triptans). Some gepants (rimegepant, atogepant) also approved for migraine PREVENTION.
categories.advantage_over_triptans: No vasoconstriction → safe in cardiovascular disease, stroke history, hemiplegic migraine; fewer 'triptan sensation' side effects

medicines.name: Ubrogepant
medicines.dosage: 50-100mg at onset; may repeat after 2 hours; max 200mg/day
medicines.use_case: Acute treatment of moderate-severe migraine with or without aura; FDA approved 2019; use in patients with cardiovascular contraindications to triptans
medicines.mechanism: CGRP receptor antagonist; blocks CGRP-mediated vasodilation and neurogenic inflammation
medicines.note: CYP3A4 interactions — avoid with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors; reduce dose with moderate inhibitors

medicines.name: Rimegepant
medicines.dosage: Acute: 75mg ODT at onset (one dose per day); Preventive: 75mg every other day
medicines.use_case: DUAL indication — FDA approved for BOTH acute treatment AND prevention of migraine; first drug approved for both uses; dissolving tablet useful with nausea; no liver toxicity concern
medicines.unique_advantage: Only medication approved for both acute treatment AND prevention of migraine in same formulation

medicines.name: Atogepant
medicines.dosage: 10-60mg once daily (prevention); 30mg or 60mg for chronic migraine
medicines.use_case: Prevention of episodic and chronic migraine; oral daily preventive gepant; effective even in patients who have failed 2-4 prior preventive medications
medicines.note: Available in India and US; growing global availability

categories.purpose: Novel class that activates 5-HT1F receptors in the trigeminal system (blocking pain transmission) without activating 5-HT1B receptors on blood vessels — NO VASOCONSTRICTION. Safe in cardiovascular disease. CNS-penetrant.

medicines.name: Lasmiditan
medicines.dosage: 50-200mg at onset; max 200mg/day
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe migraine; cardiovascular disease patients where triptans are contraindicated; FDA approved 2019
medicines.mechanism: Selective 5-HT1F agonist; binds trigeminovascular 5-HT1F receptors without vasoconstriction
side_effects: Significant CNS side effects: dizziness (most common), somnolence, fatigue, paraesthesia
DRIVING WARNING: Do not drive/operate machinery for 8 hours after dose (CNS depression)
medicines.warning: Do not drive or operate heavy machinery for 8 hours after taking — significant dizziness risk; DEA Schedule V in USA

categories.purpose: Treat nausea and vomiting during migraine attacks. Some antiemetics have independent analgesic effects for migraine (particularly dopamine antagonists). Also improve gastric motility (prokinetic effect) to enhance absorption of oral analgesics and triptans.
categories.note: Antiemetics should be taken 15-20 minutes BEFORE oral analgesics to improve gut absorption during migraine-related gastric stasis.

medicines.name: Metoclopramide
medicines.dosage: 10mg orally, 15-20 min before analgesic; 10mg IV/IM (ED setting)
medicines.use_case: First-line antiemetic for migraine; prokinetic — accelerates gastric emptying enhancing oral analgesic absorption; IV metoclopramide 10-20mg is an effective acute migraine treatment in ED setting independently
side_effects: Extrapyramidal reactions — acute dystonia (especially in young people; treat with benztropine or diphenhydramine)
medicines.note: Avoid prolonged use; maximum treatment duration 5 days

medicines.name: Domperidone
medicines.dosage: 10-20mg up to 3 times daily with meals; give before analgesics
medicines.use_case: Preferred antiemetic in children and during pregnancy (compared to metoclopramide); prokinetic; does not cross blood-brain barrier (fewer CNS extrapyramidal side effects than metoclopramide)
side_effects: QT prolongation (cardiac — use with caution in cardiac patients; avoid high doses)

medicines.name: Prochlorperazine
medicines.dosage: 5-10mg orally 3-4 times daily; 3-6mg buccal (Buccastem); 12.5mg IM; 25mg rectal
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe migraine nausea; IV prochlorperazine is highly effective in ED for acute migraine — more effective than many analgesics; buccal tablet (Buccastem) ideal for severe vomiting when oral route unavailable
medicines.mechanism: Dopamine antagonist (phenothiazine); antiemetic and mild analgesic effect
medicines.clinical_tip: IV prochlorperazine 12.5-25mg is one of the most effective ED treatments for acute migraine with vomiting

medicines.name: Ondansetron
medicines.dosage: 4-8mg orally or IV
medicines.use_case: Migraine-associated nausea/vomiting; useful when prochlorperazine contraindicated or not available; ODT wafer useful with vomiting
medicines.note: 5-HT3 antagonist — less effective as primary migraine treatment than dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)

categories.purpose: Non-selective serotonin, dopamine, and alpha-adrenergic agonists causing vasoconstriction. Older drug class; less well-tolerated than triptans; significant contraindications. Ergotamine and DHE are still useful for certain refractory or status migrainosus cases.
categories.note: Ergots have high potential for causing medication overuse headache (ergotamine-induced headache); limit to maximum 2 days per week

medicines.name: Ergotamine Tartrate + Caffeine
medicines.dosage: 1-2 tablets (ergotamine 1mg + caffeine 100mg) at onset; max 4 tablets per attack; max 6 tablets per week; suppository 1-2 at onset
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe migraine not responding to triptans or when triptans are too expensive; long attacks with risk of recurrence; NOT for hemiplegic or basilar migraine
side_effects: Ergotism (vasoconstriction of limbs — severe with overdose; gangrenous ergotism historically)
contraindications: Combination with triptans or within 24 hours of each other
Combination with CYP3A4 inhibitors (macrolides, azoles, protease inhibitors)

medicines.name: Dihydroergotamine (DHE)
medicines.dosage: IV: 0.5-1mg IV slowly; IM/SC: 1mg; Nasal: one spray (0.5mg) in each nostril, repeat after 15 min (max 3mg/24h); IV protocol: 0.5mg IV + antiemetic every 8h for 3 doses (repetitive DHE protocol for status migrainosus)
medicines.use_case: Status migrainosus (prolonged refractory migraine attack >72h); intractable migraine not responding to triptans; Raskin protocol (repetitive IV DHE); advantages: less nausea than ergotamine, less vasoconstriction, lower MOH potential than ergotamine

categories.category_name: Steroids — Acute Treatment (Adjunctive for Status Migrainosus)
categories.purpose: Adjunctive treatment for refractory migraine and status migrainosus. Dexamethasone reduces 72-hour recurrence rate; does not abort the acute attack but prevents relapse.

medicines.name: Dexamethasone
medicines.dosage: 8-16mg single IV or IM dose (or oral 6-8mg) at end of ED treatment; or single oral dose 12mg at start of severe attack
medicines.use_case: Reduces 24-72 hour headache recurrence after ED treatment; status migrainosus (>72 hours); menstrual migraine; severe acute attack
medicines.mechanism: Reduces prostaglandin synthesis; anti-inflammatory; reduces meningeal inflammation
medicines.evidence: Cochrane review: dexamethasone reduces 72-hour recurrence rate by 26% (NNT=9)

categories.purpose: Reduce migraine frequency and severity by mechanisms including: reduced adrenergic activity on trigeminal nociceptors, inhibition of cortical spreading depression, serotonergic modulation, and reduced anxiety (a migraine trigger). Most evidence-based of all preventives.
categories.indication: Preventive therapy indicated when: ≥4 migraine days/month, or ≥2 significantly disabling attacks/month, or quality of life severely impacted, or acute treatments frequently ineffective or overused

medicines.name: Propranolol
medicines.dosage: Starting: 10-20mg twice daily; usual therapeutic: 40-120mg twice daily (or 80-160mg LA once daily); titrate up over weeks
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE preventive for migraine; also treats hypertension, angina, anxiety, essential tremor — useful with these comorbidities; reduces migraine frequency by 40-50%
medicines.mechanism: Non-selective beta-1/beta-2 blocker; also inhibits 5-HT2A and 5-HT2B receptors; reduces CSD susceptibility

medicines.name: Metoprolol
medicines.dosage: 50-200mg daily
medicines.use_case: First-line preventive; cardioselective — preferred over propranolol in patients with mild asthma or COPD; also for hypertension or heart disease comorbidity

medicines.name: Atenolol
medicines.dosage: 25-100mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Once-daily dosing improves adherence for migraine prevention; cardioselective

categories.purpose: First-line preventive agents for migraine — particularly when comorbid depression, anxiety, insomnia, or chronic pain is present. Effective independent of antidepressant effects. Mechanism includes serotonin/noradrenaline reuptake inhibition, sodium channel blockade, NMDA receptor modulation.

medicines.name: Amitriptyline
medicines.dosage: Start: 10mg at night; titrate up by 10-25mg every 2-4 weeks; usual therapeutic: 25-75mg at night; max 150mg/day
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE preventive especially with: insomnia (sedating — take at night), comorbid depression, chronic daily headache, tension-type headache overlap, fibromyalgia. Reduces migraine frequency by 40-50%. Also first-line for chronic migraine.
medicines.mechanism: TCA; inhibits reuptake of serotonin and noradrenaline; NMDA receptor antagonism; sodium channel blockade; 5-HT2A receptor blockade
side_effects: Sedation and morning drowsiness (take at night; start low)
contraindications: Pregnancy (category C — use with caution; not for 1st trimester ideally)
medicines.monitoring: Baseline ECG (especially in elderly and cardiac patients); monitor BP; weight

medicines.name: Nortriptyline
medicines.dosage: 10-75mg at night
medicines.use_case: Alternative to amitriptyline; better tolerated (fewer anticholinergic side effects, less sedation); good option for elderly; also for neuropathic pain comorbidity
side_effects: Less sedation and anticholinergic effects than amitriptyline

categories.purpose: Reduce neuronal hyperexcitability and susceptibility to cortical spreading depression. Topiramate and valproate have the strongest evidence base for migraine prevention among AEDs.

medicines.name: Topiramate
medicines.dosage: Start: 25mg at night for 2 weeks; increase by 25mg every 2 weeks; usual therapeutic: 50-100mg/day (divided doses); max 200mg/day
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE preventive for migraine and chronic migraine; also approved for episodic migraine and chronic migraine; reduces migraine by 50% in 50% of patients; bonus: causes weight loss (advantageous in obese migraineurs)
medicines.mechanism: Multiple mechanisms: AMPA/kainate glutamate receptor antagonism; voltage-gated Na+ channel blockade; GABA receptor potentiation; carbonic anhydrase inhibition
side_effects: Cognitive side effects — word-finding difficulty ('tipsy-topsy'), slowed thinking (most complained of side effect)
Paresthesias — tingling fingers and toes (common, usually benign)
Kidney stones (carbonic anhydrase inhibition — drink 2-2.5L water daily)
Glaucoma (acute narrow-angle — rare but stop immediately if eye pain/vision change)
Teratogenicity — reduces efficacy of oral contraceptives; cleft lip/palate risk — AVOID in pregnancy; use contraception
medicines.monitoring: Weight, cognition, bicarbonate (metabolic acidosis), eye exam if visual symptoms

medicines.name: Sodium Valproate / Valproic Acid
medicines.form: Tablet, EC tablet, Prolonged-release tablet, Syrup
medicines.dosage: 400-1000mg daily (modified release or divided doses); start 200-400mg/day, titrate
medicines.use_case: First-line preventive; particularly useful with comorbid bipolar disorder, epilepsy, or anxiety; effective 40-50% frequency reduction
medicines.mechanism: Increases GABA neurotransmission; sodium channel blockade; reduces glutamate release; inhibits histone deacetylase
side_effects: Teratogenicity — HIGHLY TERATOGENIC (neural tube defects, cognitive impairment, autism) — ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in women of childbearing potential without highly effective contraception
contraindications: Pregnancy (ABSOLUTE — Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme mandatory in UK)
Women of childbearing age without highly effective contraception and signed informed consent
medicines.warning: EMA/MHRA: Valproate must NOT be prescribed to women of childbearing potential without signed informed consent to a pregnancy prevention programme. Fatal teratogenicity.

medicines.name: Gabapentin
medicines.dosage: 300-900mg three times daily; start 300mg at night; increase gradually
medicines.use_case: Second-line preventive; particularly useful with comorbid neuropathic pain, anxiety, or restless legs syndrome; weaker evidence than topiramate/valproate
medicines.note: Lower evidence level than topiramate or valproate; useful as add-on or when first-line agents not tolerated

categories.purpose: The most targeted preventive treatment for migraine — monoclonal antibodies specifically blocking either CGRP itself or the CGRP receptor. Designed specifically for migraine prevention. Highly effective, well-tolerated, subcutaneous monthly injection. Approved for chronic and episodic migraine refractory to previous preventives.
categories.mechanism: Block the CGRP pathway — the central mechanism of migraine. First treatments designed specifically for migraine prevention.
categories.advantage: Disease-specific; no CNS side effects; well tolerated; rapid onset (1-3 months); once-monthly SC injection; effective even after failure of multiple preventives

medicines.name: Erenumab
medicines.dosage: 70mg SC once monthly; can increase to 140mg SC once monthly if inadequate response
medicines.use_case: Prevention of episodic and chronic migraine in adults who have had inadequate response to at least 2-3 conventional preventives; FIRST anti-CGRP mAb approved (FDA 2018)
medicines.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody against CGRP RECEPTOR (anti-CGRP-R); different target from other CGRP mAbs
medicines.response_rate: 50% of patients achieve ≥50% reduction in migraine days

medicines.name: Fremanezumab
medicines.dosage: 225mg SC once monthly OR 675mg SC once every 3 months (quarterly dosing — improves adherence)
medicines.use_case: Prevention of episodic and chronic migraine; quarterly dosing option is a significant adherence advantage
medicines.unique_advantage: Quarterly (3-monthly) dosing option — 3 injections given together every 3 months

medicines.name: Galcanezumab
medicines.dosage: Loading dose 240mg SC once; then 120mg SC once monthly
medicines.use_case: Prevention of episodic and chronic migraine; cluster headache prevention (also approved); loading dose gives faster onset
medicines.unique_use: Also approved for episodic cluster headache prevention (first biologic approved for cluster headache)

medicines.name: Eptinezumab
medicines.dosage: 100mg IV infusion over 30 minutes every 3 months; some patients benefit from 300mg dose
medicines.use_case: Prevention of episodic and chronic migraine; IV delivery allows immediate onset from day of infusion; useful for very frequent/severe migraine requiring rapid effect
medicines.unique_advantage: IV administration gives immediate effect from day 1 of infusion

categories.purpose: Prevent migraine through calcium channel blockade affecting serotonin release, cortical spreading depression threshold, and vascular reactivity.

medicines.name: Flunarizine
medicines.dosage: 5-10mg at bedtime
medicines.use_case: Well-evidenced preventive; first-line in many countries (Europe, India); particularly useful with comorbid vestibular migraine; also effective for hemiplegic migraine
medicines.mechanism: Calcium channel blocker; also inhibits calmodulin and dopamine receptors
side_effects: Weight gain and increased appetite (most common — problematic)
Extrapyramidal features with prolonged use (Parkinson-like) — limit to 6-month courses
medicines.note: Very popular preventive in India and Europe; not FDA approved in USA but widely used globally

medicines.name: Verapamil
medicines.dosage: 240-480mg/day (SR formulation)
medicines.use_case: Second-line preventive for migraine; preferred for hemiplegic migraine and basilar-type migraine (beta-blockers and triptans avoided); also used in cluster headache prevention
medicines.note: Preferred preventive option for hemiplegic migraine where triptans and beta-blockers are contraindicated

categories.category_name: SNRIs and Other Antidepressants — Preventive Treatment
categories.purpose: Second-line preventive options targeting serotonin and noradrenaline pathways; particularly useful with comorbid depression, anxiety, or pain conditions.

medicines.name: Venlafaxine
medicines.dosage: 37.5-150mg once daily (XR formulation)
medicines.use_case: Second-line migraine preventive; particularly useful with comorbid depression, anxiety, or fibromyalgia; SNRI; good tolerability

medicines.name: Duloxetine
medicines.dosage: 30-60mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Second-line preventive with comorbid depression, anxiety, or fibromyalgia/chronic pain conditions

categories.category_name: Botulinum Toxin Type A (OnabotulinumtoxinA) — Preventive for Chronic Migraine
categories.purpose: The only FDA and MHRA-approved preventive treatment specifically for CHRONIC MIGRAINE. Given as 31 injections across 7 head and neck muscle areas every 12 weeks. Mechanism in migraine likely involves blocking CGRP and glutamate release from peripheral trigeminovascular afferents.

medicines.name: OnabotulinumtoxinA (Botulinum Toxin Type A)
medicines.dosage: 155-195 units divided across 31-39 injection sites in 7 head/neck muscle groups (PREEMPT protocol) every 12 weeks; administered by trained neurologist or pain specialist
medicines.use_case: APPROVED SPECIFICALLY for chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month, ≥8 migraine days/month); reduces headache days by ~8-9 per month vs ~6 with placebo; NICE approved in UK for adults with chronic migraine who have failed ≥3 preventives
medicines.mechanism: Blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction; in migraine: blocks CGRP, glutamate, and substance P release from peripheral trigeminovascular terminals; reduces peripheral sensitization
medicines.note: Effect takes 6-8 weeks to develop; full assessment after 2 treatment cycles (24 weeks); many patients continue for years

categories.category_name: ACE Inhibitors and ARBs — Preventive Treatment (Specific Indications)
categories.purpose: Second-line preventive options with additional cardiovascular benefit; useful when beta-blockers contraindicated.

medicines.name: Candesartan
medicines.dosage: 8-16mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Second-line preventive particularly useful when beta-blockers contraindicated (asthma, diabetes, Raynaud's); also treats hypertension; RCT evidence for 40% frequency reduction
medicines.note: CANPAIN trial showed candesartan as effective as propranolol for migraine prevention

medicines.name: Lisinopril
medicines.dosage: 10-20mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Second-line preventive; ACE inhibitor with migraine prevention evidence; also treats hypertension
side_effects: ACEi cough (class effect — switch to candesartan if cough develops)

categories.purpose: Several nutritional supplements have Grade A or B evidence for migraine prevention in clinical guidelines. Safer profile than pharmacological preventives — important for patients who prefer non-pharmacological approaches, cannot tolerate drugs, or are pregnant.

medicines.name: Magnesium Oxide / Magnesium Citrate
medicines.dosage: 400-600mg elemental magnesium daily (magnesium citrate or glycinate preferred for absorption and tolerability); American Headache Society: Grade A evidence
medicines.use_case: Preventive for episodic migraine; PARTICULARLY EFFECTIVE for menstrual migraine (magnesium deficiency common pre-menstrually); safe in pregnancy; important adjunct for all migraineurs
medicines.mechanism: Magnesium stabilises NMDA receptors; reduces cortical spreading depression susceptibility; reduces platelet aggregation; opposes calcium-induced vasoconstriction; deficiency demonstrated in migraineurs (low ionised Mg2+ in serum and CSF)
side_effects: Diarrhoea (most common — loose stools; magnesium citrate gentler than oxide)
medicines.evidence: Multiple RCTs show magnesium supplementation reduces migraine frequency by 40-50%; AHS Grade A; first-line in pregnancy

medicines.name: Riboflavin (Vitamin B2)
brand_examples: Various B-complex vitamins; standalone riboflavin 400mg capsules
medicines.dosage: 400mg once daily (high dose required — far above dietary RDA of 1.3mg)
medicines.use_case: Preventive for episodic migraine; safe in pregnancy; European guidelines Grade A recommendation; takes 3 months for full effect
medicines.mechanism: Riboflavin is a precursor of FAD and FMN — essential cofactors for mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. Migraine may involve mitochondrial energy deficit in neurons — riboflavin improves mitochondrial energy production and reduces neuronal hyperexcitability
side_effects: Bright yellow/orange urine (harmless riboflavinuria — reassure patient)
Mild GI upset at very high doses
medicines.evidence: Schoenen et al. RCT: 400mg/day reduced migraine frequency by 50% in 59% of patients

medicines.name: Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10 / Ubiquinone)
medicines.dosage: 300-400mg daily (3 × 100mg doses preferred for absorption; or 300mg once daily with food)
medicines.use_case: Preventive for migraine; AHS Grade B evidence; particularly with riboflavin and magnesium (triple supplementation); safe in pregnancy
medicines.mechanism: Mitochondrial electron transport chain component; improves mitochondrial energy production; antioxidant; anti-inflammatory
medicines.evidence: Sandor et al. RCT: 300mg/day CoQ10 reduced migraine frequency by 48%; AHS Grade B

medicines.name: Melatonin
medicines.dosage: 3mg at bedtime
medicines.use_case: Preventive for migraine, particularly in patients with sleep disorders (sleep disturbance is a major trigger); free radical scavenger; anti-inflammatory; comparable to amitriptyline in some studies with better tolerability
medicines.evidence: Gonçalves et al. RCT: melatonin 3mg comparable to amitriptyline 25mg for migraine prevention with better tolerability

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet plays a crucial dual role in migraine management: (1) identifying and avoiding individual dietary triggers and (2) consuming nutrients that reduce neuronal excitability and migraine susceptibility. Magnesium deficiency is the single most important nutritional factor in migraine — low intracellular and CSF magnesium has been demonstrated in migraineurs. A ketogenic or low-glycaemic diet may reduce migraine frequency. Keeping a food diary to identify personal triggers is essential.

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — Grade A clinical guideline recommendation for magnesium supplementation in migraine prevention. Migraineurs demonstrate lower intracellular magnesium levels. Magnesium stabilises NMDA receptors, reduces cortical spreading depression susceptibility, and inhibits platelet aggregation.

items.benefit: Highest food magnesium content; 1 cup cooked spinach provides ~157mg magnesium; potassium; anti-inflammatory

items.frequency: Half an avocado 4-5 times per week

items.frequency: 1 daily if not triggering

items.benefit: High EPA and DHA omega-3; reduce CGRP levels; anti-inflammatory; reduce platelet aggregation; reduce triglycerides (elevated in migraineurs)

items.caution: Avoid smoked, pickled, or canned fish — high in tyramine and histamine (triggers)

items.benefit: ALA omega-3; also fibre and magnesium; anti-inflammatory; reduce brain inflammation underlying migraine

items.benefit: ALA omega-3; magnesium; anti-inflammatory; but note: some patients report walnuts as a trigger — monitor

Study: ginger powder 250mg as effective as sumatriptan 50mg for acute migraine (Maghbooli et al. 2014)
items.evidence: Grade B for acute treatment; traditional and emerging evidence
items.frequency: Fresh ginger tea (1 inch fresh ginger in hot water) at attack onset; daily 1-2 cups preventively
items.use: First treatment to try at onset of migraine — anti-nausea and analgesic properties

items.benefit: Curcumin inhibits NF-κB inflammatory pathway; reduces CGRP production; anti-inflammatory effects on trigeminal nerve activation; emerging evidence for migraine prevention
items.frequency: Daily in cooking, golden milk, or supplement (500-1000mg curcumin with piperine twice daily)

items.benefit: Anthocyanins reduce neurogenic inflammation; reduce oxidative stress in brain; antioxidant protection against trigeminovascular inflammatory cascade; melatonin in tart cherries supports sleep
items.frequency: Daily — 1 cup; tart cherry juice beneficial

items.benefit: Dehydration is one of the most consistent and avoidable migraine triggers. Even mild dehydration (1-2% body weight loss) triggers attacks in susceptible individuals. Adequate hydration may abort attacks early. Electrolyte-containing water during attacks with vomiting.
items.target: Adults: 2-2.5 litres daily (8-10 glasses); more in hot weather, with exercise, or with caffeine use
items.frequency: Consistently throughout the day — do not wait to feel thirsty
items.tip: Keep a water bottle visible as a constant reminder; dehydration headache often mistaken for migraine

items.food: Herbal teas: Ginger tea, Chamomile, Lavender, Peppermint
items.benefit: Hydration + specific therapeutic benefits: ginger (anti-nausea), chamomile (anti-inflammatory, relaxing), lavender (analgesic, anxiolytic), peppermint (analgesic — topical menthol on temples also shown to reduce migraine pain)
items.frequency: 2-3 cups daily; ginger tea at migraine onset
