items.food: Protein with each meal: Legumes, Eggs, Low-fat dairy, Fish, Tofu, Lentils
items.benefit: Protein slows glucose absorption; maintains stable blood sugar; prevents hypoglycaemia (a major trigger); amino acids (tryptophan) for serotonin synthesis
items.frequency: Include protein source with every meal and snack

items.food: Complex carbohydrates: Oats, Brown rice, Whole wheat, Sweet potato, Quinoa
items.benefit: Low glycaemic index — slow, sustained glucose release; prevents the blood sugar peaks and crashes that trigger migraine
items.frequency: Prefer over refined white carbohydrates at all meals

items.food: Regular snacks to prevent skipping meals
items.benefit: Skipping meals is a top migraine trigger — even a 4-5 hour gap without food can trigger an attack in susceptible individuals. Regular small meals and healthy snacks maintain stable blood glucose.
items.frequency: 3 main meals + 2 snacks daily; never skip breakfast

foods_to_avoid.food: Alcohol — Especially Red Wine and Beer
foods_to_avoid.reason: Most potent dietary migraine trigger. Red wine: contains histamine, tyramine, flavonoids, and sulfites. Beer: contains histamine and yeast (tyramine source). Even small amounts (1-2 drinks) trigger attacks within 3 hours in most migraineurs. White wine and vodka are less triggering but still problematic for many.
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Complete avoidance strongly recommended for migraineurs, especially during preventive treatment.

foods_to_avoid.reason: Tyramine — a biogenic amine formed during cheese ageing — releases catecholamines and serotonin. Blocks monoamine oxidase (MAO). Strong, aged cheeses have the highest tyramine content.

foods_to_avoid.food: Processed and Cured Meats (Nitrates and Tyramine)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Nitrates and nitrites (preservatives) are directly vasodilatory — they trigger nitric oxide release causing meningeal vasodilation. Also high in tyramine.
examples: Any cured, smoked, or pickled meat
foods_to_avoid.safe_alternatives: Fresh, unprocessed lean meats; grilled chicken; fresh fish

foods_to_avoid.reason: MSG is an excitatory amino acid (glutamate) that may over-activate trigeminovascular neurons. Classic 'Chinese restaurant headache' — headache 20-30 minutes after MSG-containing meal. Also hidden in many processed foods under different names.
hidden_sources: Listed as: 'natural flavors', 'hydrolyzed vegetable protein', 'autolyzed yeast', 'glutamate'

foods_to_avoid.reason: Aspartame is metabolised to phenylalanine, aspartic acid (excitatory), and methanol. Multiple patient reports and some case-control studies link aspartame to migraine triggering. Many migraineurs report marked improvement after eliminating diet sodas.
examples: Artificial sweeteners: aspartame (Equal, NutraSweet), sucralose (Splenda) — less evidence but some reports

foods_to_avoid.reason: Complex role in migraine: (1) In small amounts, caffeine potentiates analgesics and can HELP an acute attack (component of Excedrin Migraine). (2) Regular caffeine use creates dependence — caffeine withdrawal is one of the most consistent migraine triggers (missing morning coffee). (3) Excessive caffeine causes rebound headaches. Recommendation: maintain stable daily intake OR gradually reduce to zero.
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: If reducing caffeine: decrease by no more than 25mg (1/4 cup coffee) per week to prevent withdrawal headaches; do not stop abruptly

foods_to_avoid.reason: Some migraineurs have reduced diamine oxidase (DAO) enzyme activity — unable to break down dietary histamine efficiently. Histamine causes vasodilation and activates pain receptors. A low-histamine diet helps a subset of migraineurs.
high_histamine_foods: Fermented foods: kimchi, sauerkraut, kefir, vinegar
Canned and smoked fish (sardines, tuna, mackerel — canned)
Leftovers (histamine accumulates as food ages — eat fresh)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) from meal skipping is one of the most consistent and avoidable migraine triggers. Even a 4-5 hour gap without food during waking hours triggers attacks. Intermittent fasting and very-low-calorie diets commonly worsen migraine frequency.
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Never skip meals; breakfast is critical; eat every 3-4 hours; always carry a healthy snack

foods_to_avoid.reason: Alcohol and excess caffeine cause diuresis and dehydration — both direct migraine triggers.

sample_meal_plan.note: This low-tyramine, magnesium-rich, anti-inflammatory migraine-prevention meal plan avoids common triggers. Individual triggers vary greatly — use a headache diary to identify your specific triggers. Maintain regular meal timing and NEVER skip meals.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning: Upon waking: 2 large glasses of water (prevent dehydration) + fresh ginger slice in warm water + 10-12 soaked almonds (magnesium) or pumpkin seeds
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Oatmeal with fresh banana slices, ground flaxseed, and blueberries (no dried/preserved fruit — high tyramine) + 1-2 boiled or scrambled eggs + glass of skimmed milk or fortified almond milk + 1 cup ginger or chamomile herbal tea
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: 1 apple or pear (fresh — no dried) + 1 tbsp almond butter OR a small pot of plain yogurt with honey
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Brown rice or whole wheat chapati (2) + moong dal or chana dal (magnesium + low-GI) + fresh spinach sabzi with garlic and olive oil + fresh tomato and cucumber raita (avoid vinegar-based dressings) + plain fresh curd
sample_meal_plan.evening_snack: A small handful of unsalted mixed nuts (almonds, walnuts — if not triggering) + 1 cup warm ginger or peppermint tea OR fresh fruit (apple, pear, mango in season — avoid citrus if triggering)
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Grilled fresh fish (salmon or mackerel) or paneer with vegetables + quinoa or brown rice + steamed broccoli with olive oil + fresh green salad (no balsamic vinegar — use lemon dressing) + glass of water
sample_meal_plan.before_bed: Warm low-fat milk (calcium + tryptophan for serotonin synthesis and sleep) with 1/2 tsp turmeric OR chamomile tea; ensure 7-8 hours of sleep at consistent time

special_dietary_notes: MAGNESIUM is the single most important dietary intervention — ensure 400-600mg supplemental magnesium daily (magnesium citrate or glycinate for best absorption and tolerability); even with a good diet, supplements are usually needed to reach therapeutic levels
Keep a MIGRAINE DIARY recording all foods eaten in 24-48 hours before each attack — builds a personalised trigger list; what triggers one person may not trigger another
Regular meal timing is as important as what you eat — hypoglycaemia from delayed meals is one of the most avoidable triggers; eat every 3-4 hours
Low-glycaemic diet: multiple RCTs show ketogenic and low-GI diets reduce migraine frequency by 50-70% — likely through reduced neuronal excitability and improved mitochondrial function
CAFFEINE MANAGEMENT: If you drink coffee, maintain a consistent daily amount at a consistent time. Do not vary intake — both excess caffeine and caffeine withdrawal trigger migraine.
Riboflavin 400mg/day supplement: difficult to achieve therapeutically from diet alone — take as supplement. Safe in pregnancy. Note bright yellow urine — harmless.
Omega-3 fish oil supplement: if fish consumption inadequate, take 2-4g EPA+DHA fish oil daily with food; reduces migraine frequency in RCTs.
Tryptophan-rich foods (turkey, eggs, dairy, bananas, oats) support serotonin synthesis — important for migraine pathophysiology.
Anti-histamine diet trial: If conventional trigger avoidance does not reduce migraines, trial a low-histamine diet for 4 weeks — helps in DAO-deficient migraineurs.
Hydration: 2-2.5 litres water daily; increase with hot weather, exercise, or caffeine consumption; electrolyte drink if vomiting during attacks

sleep_hygiene.importance: Sleep is one of the most powerful triggers AND treatments for migraine. Both too little sleep (sleep deprivation) and too much sleep (oversleeping at weekends) trigger attacks. The hypothalamus — the 'migraine generator' — governs sleep-wake cycles, explaining the strong link.
sleep_hygiene.sleep_targets: 7-8 hours per night; consistent wake and sleep time every day (even weekends — 'social jet lag' from weekend oversleeping is a major trigger)
recommendations: Maintain exactly the same sleep and wake time every day — including weekends (most important measure)
Avoid napping during the day (disrupts night-time sleep quality and circadian rhythm)
Create a dark, cool, quiet sleep environment (22-24°C); blackout curtains
No screens (phone, tablet, TV) for 60-90 minutes before bedtime — blue light suppresses melatonin
Avoid alcohol — disrupts deep sleep quality despite seeming to cause drowsiness
If migraine wakes you at night, take your acute medication immediately rather than waiting until morning
Sleep restriction therapy (CBT-I) for insomnia — improving sleep quality significantly reduces migraine frequency

stress_management.importance: Stress is the most commonly reported migraine trigger (50-70%). Two distinct mechanisms: (1) Stress itself activates the HPA axis, releases cortisol and adrenaline triggering attacks; (2) 'Let-down' headache — migraine occurs on relaxation after stress (Friday evening migraine, holiday migraine).
techniques: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) for headache — strong evidence; reduces migraine frequency by 35-50%; address catastrophising and pain anxiety
Biofeedback — thermal biofeedback or EMG biofeedback; Grade A evidence for migraine prevention; teaches autonomic self-regulation
Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) — mindfulness specifically adapted for chronic pain; reduces migraine frequency and improves disability
Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR) — systematic relaxation of muscle groups; reduces pericranial muscle tension (significant in tension-type headache overlap with migraine)
Diaphragmatic deep breathing — slow breathing (6 breaths/min); activates parasympathetic nervous system; can be used during prodrome to potentially abort attack
Regular yoga — reduces stress, improves cervical flexibility, reduces sympathetic tone; evidence shows yoga reduces migraine frequency
Establish 'stress buffer' activities: hobbies, social connection, time in nature, music — preventing complete stress buildup

exercise.importance: Regular aerobic exercise is Grade B preventive treatment for migraine. Exercise releases endorphins (natural pain modulators), reduces CGRP, improves sleep, reduces anxiety/depression (major comorbidities), and reduces body weight (obesity = migraine risk factor). Paradox: intense exercise can TRIGGER attacks while regular moderate exercise PREVENTS them.
recommended: Brisk walking — 30-45 min, 3-5 days per week; most accessible; low trigger risk
Cycling (steady pace) — low impact; effective aerobic exercise; good in climate-controlled environment
Swimming — water provides head support; minimal head movement; cooling effect; excellent for migraine
Yoga — dual benefits of aerobic and stress reduction; evidence specifically for migraine
Jogging or running at moderate, consistent pace (not sprint intervals)
precautions: Avoid vigorous exercise during prodrome or early attack — exercise at that phase triggers full attacks
Warm up gradually (10 min) — abrupt onset of intense exercise triggers exertional migraine
Stay well-hydrated before, during, and after exercise — dehydration during exercise is a strong trigger
Exercise in cool, well-ventilated environments — heat worsens headache
If exercise regularly triggers migraine: take NSAID or triptan 30-60 min before exercise (discuss with neurologist)

migraine_diary.importance: A migraine diary is the single most important self-management tool — it tracks headache days, severity, triggers, symptoms, medications used, and their effectiveness. Essential for establishing correct diagnosis, identifying personal triggers, monitoring treatment response, and screening for medication overuse headache (MOH).
what_to_record: Date and time of headache onset and resolution
Associated symptoms: aura (describe), nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia
Medications taken: name, dose, time taken, effectiveness (0-10)
Possible triggers: foods eaten in previous 24-48h, sleep hours, stress level, menstrual phase (women), weather, physical activity
Disability: missed work, limited activity (calculate MIDAS monthly)
migraine_diary.apps: Digital diary apps: Migraine Buddy (most popular), N1-Headache, Healow, MyMigraine (AHS/AAN approved apps improve diary accuracy vs paper)

trigger_avoidance_strategies: Maintain stable sleep-wake schedule (most important single lifestyle measure)
Eat regularly — never skip meals; carry emergency snacks; eat within 30-60 min of waking
Maintain consistent caffeine intake or gradually reduce to zero
Wear sunglasses outdoors (UV and glare filter); use blue-light filter apps on screens (f.lux, Night Shift)
Use polarised lenses if driving is triggering
Tinted glasses with FL-41 lens tint specifically for photophobia and fluorescent light sensitivity
Avoid strong perfumes and fragrances; use fragrance-free products; inform workplace colleagues
HEPA air purifier at home and work to reduce chemical vapours and allergens
Monitor barometric pressure via weather app — prepare rescue medication when pressure drops forecast
Identify and manage hormonal triggers (menstrual diary in women; discuss hormonal management with gynaecologist)

devices.name: Cefaly
devices.use: Both acute (20 min at attack onset) and preventive (20 min daily) treatment; FDA cleared; stimulates supraorbital branch of trigeminal nerve
devices.evidence: ACME trial: acute mode reduced pain at 2 hours; preventive mode reduced frequency by 30%

devices.name: gammaCore (Nuvana)
devices.use: Acute treatment (applied to neck over vagus nerve for 2 min); preventive treatment (3 daily stimulations); FDA cleared for migraine and cluster headache
devices.evidence: Reduces acute attack pain; reduces frequency in episodic migraine

devices.name: sTMS mini (Spring TMS / eNeura)
devices.use: Acute treatment: apply to back of head at aura onset; preventive: 4 pulses twice daily; FDA cleared

non_pharmacological_treatments.evidence: Cochrane review: acupuncture reduces migraine frequency at least as effectively as prophylactic drug treatment; Grade A NICE recommendation for migraine prevention
non_pharmacological_treatments.protocol: 10-16 sessions over 5-8 weeks; traditional acupuncture or dry needling of trigger points
non_pharmacological_treatments.note: Considered as preventive treatment when pharmacological options are contraindicated or not tolerated (pregnancy, elderly, patient preference)

non_pharmacological_treatments.evidence: Moderate — cervical spine manual therapy, massage, and physiotherapy significantly reduce migraine frequency when cervicogenic component present
non_pharmacological_treatments.technique: Suboccipital muscle release; cervical mobilisation; posture correction; trigger point therapy for pericranial muscles; therapeutic taping

non_pharmacological_treatments.evidence: Moderate — RCT evidence: 10% peppermint oil applied topically to forehead and temples at attack onset comparably effective to paracetamol 1g for acute pain relief
non_pharmacological_treatments.use: Apply diluted peppermint oil to forehead, temples, and neck at headache onset; cooling sensation activates TRPM8 receptors providing analgesia

acute_self_management_at_attack_onset: Take acute medication IMMEDIATELY — do not wait for headache to peak (earlier = more effective); first sign of pain or recognising prodrome warning signs
Drink 2-3 glasses of water immediately — dehydration worsening is preventable
Take prescribed antiemetic 15-20 min before oral analgesic (improves absorption)
Move to dark, quiet, cool room — reduce sensory stimulation
Apply cold compress or ice pack to forehead or back of neck
Apply topical peppermint oil to temples and forehead
Lie down with eyes closed — movement worsens pain
Sleep if possible — sleep often resolves migraine attack
Avoid strong odours — remove air fresheners, leave rooms with cooking smells
If vomiting occurs: use non-oral medication routes (nasal spray triptan, IM antiemetic, rectal suppository, dissolving tablet)

migraine_monitoring_plan.note: Migraine monitoring combines headache diary tracking with validated questionnaires. The goal of preventive treatment is ≥50% reduction in migraine days per month. Monthly review of diary data guides treatment decisions.

green_zone.criteria: ≤4 migraine days per month; MIDAS Grade I or II; HIT-6 score <56; acute medications required on ≤10 days per month; no disability; good quality of life
green_zone.action: Continue current preventive and acute medication regimens. Maintain headache diary. Review with neurologist/GP every 3-6 months. Continue lifestyle measures. If stable ≥12 months, consider trial reduction of preventive therapy.

yellow_zone.criteria: 5-14 migraine days per month; MIDAS Grade III (moderate disability); acute medication use approaching 10 days/month; preventive medicine inadequate response after 3 months; missing work or social events regularly
yellow_zone.action: Contact neurologist or GP within 2-4 weeks. Review headache diary: Is there medication overuse? Are triggers identified and avoided? Dose increase or change of preventive medication likely needed. Consider CGRP mAb referral if 2+ preventives have failed.

red_zone.criteria_for_urgent_care: Any of: headache lasting >72 hours without relief (status migrainosus) — go to emergency department; headache described as worst ever/thunderclap — rule out SAH; neurological symptoms (facial weakness, one-sided limb weakness, speech difficulty, vision loss) — possible stroke; fever + headache + neck stiffness — possible meningitis; headache in pregnancy — possible eclampsia
red_zone.criteria_for_early_review: ≥15 headache days per month (chronic migraine); analgesic use >10-15 days/month (possible MOH); complete failure of 2+ preventive therapies; significant disability (MIDAS Grade IV); new or worsening aura symptoms
red_zone.action: For neurological emergency signs — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY (stroke protocol). For status migrainosus >72h — go to emergency department. For chronic migraine assessment — urgent neurology referral. For MOH — supervised medication withdrawal under neurologist guidance.

complications.description: Transformation from episodic migraine (≤14 days/month) to chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month) through gradual progression. Affects ~3% of population; 1.5 million in UK alone. Major driver is medication overuse headache. Severely disabling — loss of employment, social isolation, psychiatric comorbidities.
complications.risk_factors: Frequent episodic migraine, medication overuse, obesity, anxiety/depression, sleep disorders, stressful life events
complications.management: Preventive therapy (CGRP mAbs, botulinum toxin); medication withdrawal for MOH; multidisciplinary pain management; psychological support

complications.description: A paradoxical complication of frequent use of acute headache medications — taking triptans, NSAIDs, or combination analgesics on ≥10 days/month causes central sensitization and neuroplastic changes that produce an almost-daily headache. The headache becomes dependent on the medication. Affects 1-2% of the general population and up to 30% of headache clinic patients.
complications.causative_medications: Opioids and combination analgesics (>10 days/month); triptans (>10 days/month); NSAIDs (>15 days/month)
complications.severity: Moderate-severe; very refractory to standard treatment
complications.management: Withdrawal of overused medication (supervised; headache typically worsens for 7-14 days then dramatically improves); bridge therapy during withdrawal (prednisolone, IV dihydroergotamine, naproxen); preventive medication; psychological support for the withdrawal process

complications.description: Rare (< 0.5% of migraineurs) — ischaemic stroke that occurs during a migraine with aura attack, with neurological deficits persisting beyond 60 minutes and confirmed infarct on neuroimaging in the migraine-relevant territory.
complications.risk_factors: Migraine with aura + oral contraceptive pill + smoking — powerful triple risk combination; hypertension; hypercoagulable states; PFO (patent foramen ovale)
complications.severity: Severe — can cause permanent neurological disability
complications.prevention: Stop smoking; avoid OCP (especially with aura); control hypertension; screen for PFO; aspirin; preventive migraine treatment

complications.description: Aura symptoms (most commonly visual) persisting for more than 1 week without neuroimaging evidence of infarction. Can persist for months or years. Not fully understood — possibly related to sustained CSD or cortical dysfunction.
complications.severity: Moderate — disability from persistent visual symptoms
complications.management: Specialist referral; exclude other causes; SSRI, valproate, or lamotrigine may help

complications.description: Migraine, depression, and anxiety are bidirectionally linked — migraineurs have 2-5x higher lifetime prevalence of depression and anxiety vs general population. This bidirectionality is mediated by shared serotonin, noradrenaline, and glutamate pathways. Psychiatric comorbidity worsens migraine outcomes and disability.
complications.severity: Moderate — significantly worsens migraine prognosis and quality of life
complications.management: Screen every migraineur for depression (PHQ-9) and anxiety (GAD-7); amitriptyline or venlafaxine are preferred preventives in this setting (dual benefit); CBT; SSRI/SNRI for severe psychiatric comorbidity; suicide risk assessment

complications.description: Extremely rare — seizure occurring during or within 1 hour of migraine aura. Migraine aura may lower the seizure threshold in susceptible individuals. Also known as 'migralepsy'. Requires EEG evaluation and anticonvulsant therapy.

A single migraine attack lasting more than 72 hours despite standard treatment. Severely debilitating; causes significant dehydration; often requires emergency department visit and parenteral treatment. May be precipitated by analgesic rebound or intercurrent illness.
complications.management: Emergency department: IV antiemetics (prochlorperazine, metoclopramide), IV dihydroergotamine, IV ketorolac, IV dexamethasone, IV fluids; hospital admission if refractory

complications.description: Vestibular migraine is the most common cause of recurrent spontaneous vertigo. Chronic vestibular dysfunction can develop — persistent dizziness, imbalance, and spatial disorientation. Significantly impairs driving, employment, and quality of life.
complications.management: Migraine-specific preventives; vestibular rehabilitation physiotherapy; betahistine for symptom management

complications.complication: Cutaneous Allodynia and Central Sensitization Syndrome
complications.description: Repeated migraine attacks progressively increase central sensitization — lowering pain thresholds throughout the body. Allodynia (normally painless stimuli are painful — wearing glasses, combing hair, lying on a pillow) affects up to 70% of chronic migraineurs. Predicts poor acute treatment response (triptans less effective once allodynia present) and progression to chronic migraine.
complications.severity: Moderate — chronic; bidirectional relationship with migraine frequency

key_points: Migraine affects 7-10% of school-age children; up to 28% of adolescents
Headache in children is often bilateral (frontal or temporal) — unlike adult unilateral pattern; duration 1-72 hours (minimum 1 hour)
GI symptoms are particularly prominent in children — significant nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain
Childhood migraine equivalents: cyclical vomiting syndrome, abdominal migraine, benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood — these may precede typical migraine by years
Acute treatment: ibuprofen 10mg/kg (first-line); paracetamol 15mg/kg; sumatriptan nasal spray licensed from age 12 in many countries; almotriptan approved from 12 years
Preventive treatment: propranolol (first-line); topiramate (licensed 12+ years); amitriptyline (low dose); cyproheptadine (antihistamine — useful especially in younger children for prevention)
Screen for anxiety and depression — very common comorbidities in paediatric migraine; anxiety often the primary driver
School management: medication plan; permission to rest in dark room; regular attendance monitoring
Lifestyle interventions first: sleep schedule, hydration, meal timing, screen time reduction — more powerful in children than adults
Valproate is AVOIDED in girls and women of childbearing age due to teratogenicity risk
Migraine typically IMPROVES in 2nd and 3rd trimester (due to rising stable oestrogen) — 50-70% of migraineurs improve in pregnancy
First trimester may worsen or be unchanged
Postpartum period: migraine frequently relapses severely within days of delivery (oestrogen drop)
SAFE acute treatments in pregnancy: Paracetamol (first-line, all trimesters); Metoclopramide (antiemetic — first-line); Ibuprofen (2nd trimester only — avoid 1st and 3rd trimester)

AVOID in pregnancy: Triptans (limited safety data; not recommended by most guidelines though sumatriptan pregnancy registry shows no increased risk); Ergotamine (uterotonic — CONTRAINDICATED); NSAIDs in 1st trimester and after 20 weeks; codeine (risk of neonatal withdrawal)

SAFE preventive options in pregnancy: Magnesium oxide/citrate (strong evidence; safe all trimesters); Riboflavin 400mg (safe); CoQ10 (generally considered safe); Melatonin 3mg (limited but reassuring data)

AVOID preventive medications in pregnancy: Topiramate (teratogenic — oral clefts); Valproate (highly teratogenic — ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED); Amitriptyline (used with caution 2nd trimester only); Beta-blockers (fetal growth restriction with prolonged use; labetalol specifically the safest beta-blocker in pregnancy)
Acupuncture: safe and effective non-pharmacological preventive option in pregnancy
Postpartum: restart preventive therapy immediately; many triptans are compatible with breastfeeding (check individual drug; sumatriptan generally considered safe while breastfeeding — WHO compatible)
If migraine is severe and disabling despite safe options: specialist referral; risk-benefit discussion with obstetrician and neurologist
Women experience migraine 3x more than men due to oestrogen fluctuations (oestrogen is a migraine modulator)
Menarche: migraine often begins at puberty when hormonal cycles begin
Menstrual migraine: attacks around menstruation are most severe, longest, most treatment-resistant; managed with frovatriptan/naratriptan mini-prophylaxis or oestrogen supplementation perimenstrually

Oral contraceptives: combined OCP (oestrogen + progestogen) can worsen migraine with aura; progestogen-only pill (POP/mini-pill) is safer; AVOID combined OCP in migraine with aura (increased stroke risk — WHO category 3-4)
Pregnancy: see separate section
Perimenopause: migraine often worsens significantly as oestrogen levels fluctuate widely during perimenopause; particularly challenging to manage
Menopause: surgical menopause (bilateral oophorectomy) causes abrupt oestrogen drop — often worsens migraine; natural menopause → most migraineurs improve after menopause

HRT in menopause: oestrogen patches or gels (transdermal — avoids peaks and troughs of oral) with continuous progestogen preferred if HRT needed; avoid oral oestrogen in migraine with aura (stroke risk)
Migraine prevalence decreases with age — only 5-10% of people over 70 years have active migraine
Presentation may become atypical: aura without headache ('acephalalgic migraine') becomes more common with advancing age
New headache in elderly MUST exclude serious secondary causes: giant cell arteritis, subdural haematoma, brain tumour, stroke
Triptans in elderly: use with caution; screen for cardiovascular contraindications carefully
Medication interactions more common — polypharmacy common; check for drug interactions with amitriptyline (anticholinergic burden), propranolol, and topiramate
Cognitive impairment (topiramate side effect) may be more pronounced in elderly
Amitriptyline side effects (sedation, orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention) more significant in elderly — use minimum effective dose
Renal and hepatic function affect drug metabolism and dosing
Melatonin 3mg may be particularly beneficial in elderly migraine with sleep disorder

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Viral infections including influenza are significant migraine triggers (immune activation, fever, and systemic inflammation trigger attacks). Annual flu vaccination reduces both flu illness and the migraine attacks it would trigger. Particularly important for frequent migraineurs.

COVID-19 infection causes severe headache (new daily persistent headache and worsened migraine in Long COVID); vaccination reduces severity and duration of COVID-19 illness. Note: some migraineurs report a migraine attack as a transient post-vaccination reaction — manageable with standard acute treatment.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Per national schedule; priority for adults ≥50 or with chronic conditions
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Bacterial meningitis causes severe headache that must be differentiated from migraine; pneumococcal vaccination reduces risk of bacterial meningitis. Migraineurs with structural or neurological comorbidities (immunosuppressed on preventive biologics) are at higher risk.

Meningococcal meningitis presents with severe headache, fever, and neck stiffness — can mimic or complicate migraine assessment. Vaccination recommended per national schedule particularly in adolescents (school/college entry).
Routine adult immunisation; pertussis illness and high fever can trigger severe migraine attacks in susceptible individuals.

Standard adult immunization; women on topiramate or valproate for migraine prevention require careful contraception planning — both reduce OCP efficacy. Women should be offered HPV vaccination regardless of migraine treatment.

when_to_see_doctor: First-ever severe headache — especially if sudden in onset, 'thunderclap', or worst headache of life — requires IMMEDIATE evaluation (rule out subarachnoid haemorrhage)
Headaches that are progressively increasing in frequency or severity over weeks to months
Migraine frequency reaching ≥4 days per month — preventive therapy should be assessed
Using acute headache medications (analgesics, triptans) on more than 10 days per month — possible medication overuse headache (MOH) developing
Aura symptoms lasting more than 60 minutes or headache not following aura — possible TIA
New neurological symptoms with headache: arm or leg weakness, facial drooping, speech difficulty, sudden vision loss — possible stroke
Headache associated with fever, neck stiffness, and photophobia — possible meningitis
Headache waking you from sleep regularly (not standard migraine pattern — requires investigation)
Significant change in headache character — new location, different quality, more severe
Headache with new or worsening visual changes
Headache in pregnancy or within 6 weeks of childbirth — possible pre-eclampsia or cerebral venous thrombosis
Two or more preventive medications have failed — specialist neurology referral for CGRP mAbs or botulinum toxin
Significant impact on work, relationships, or daily functioning (MIDAS Grade III or IV) — warrants specialist input
Concerns about medications: pregnancy, medication interactions, side effects of current preventives
emergency_signs: Thunderclap headache — sudden onset severe headache reaching maximum intensity within 1 minute (worst headache ever experienced) — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES: subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise
Headache with fever (>38°C), neck stiffness, sensitivity to light — possible bacterial meningitis or encephalitis — EMERGENCY
Headache with new focal neurological symptoms: face, arm, or leg weakness; slurred speech; aphasia — possible stroke (FAST: Face, Arms, Speech, Time) — EMERGENCY
Sudden severe vision loss in one eye — retinal artery occlusion or acute stroke — EMERGENCY
Headache with confusion, decreased consciousness, or seizures — hypertensive encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, or encephalitis — EMERGENCY
New severe headache in elderly patient over 50 with scalp tenderness and jaw pain — giant cell arteritis — urgent same-day assessment to prevent blindness
Severe headache in pregnant women (especially after 20 weeks) or postpartum with visual changes or oedema — possible eclampsia — OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY
Status migrainosus — migraine lasting more than 72 hours without relief — attend emergency department for parenteral treatment
Aura symptoms lasting more than 60 minutes without resolving — possible TIA or stroke — EMERGENCY
Post-traumatic headache following head injury worsening rather than improving — possible intracranial haemorrhage or CSF leak — EMERGENCY

frequently_asked_questions.question: What exactly is a migraine and how is it different from a regular headache?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Migraine is a complex neurological disorder — not simply a bad headache. It involves a cascade of brain events including cortical spreading depression (a wave of neural activity), activation of the trigeminal pain system, neurogenic inflammation, and release of CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide). A migraine attack lasts 4-72 hours, causes moderate-severe throbbing pain (usually one-sided), and is accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and extreme sensitivity to light and sound. Regular tension headaches are bilateral, pressing/squeezing, mild-moderate, and without these associated features.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is a migraine aura?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Migraine aura is a transient neurological symptom lasting 5-60 minutes that precedes or accompanies the headache in about 25-30% of migraineurs. The most common aura is visual — typically a 'scintillating scotoma': a bright crescent of zigzag flickering lights ('fortification spectra') that slowly expands across the visual field over 20-30 minutes, leaving a blank area. Sensory aura causes tingling/numbness spreading from fingers to face. Speech aura causes word-finding difficulty. Aura is caused by cortical spreading depression — a slow wave of neuronal depolarisation across the brain.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What causes migraine attacks?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Migraines are triggered by specific factors ('triggers') activating the trigeminovascular pain system in a brain that is predisposed through genetics. Common triggers include: menstruation (oestrogen drop), stress and relaxation after stress (weekend migraine), disrupted sleep (too much or too little), skipping meals or dehydration, alcohol (especially red wine), strong smells, bright or flickering lights, and barometric pressure changes. Identifying your personal triggers through a migraine diary is one of the most effective management strategies.

frequently_asked_questions.question: When should I take my migraine medication?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Take your acute medication as EARLY as possible — at the first sign of a headache or when you recognise prodrome symptoms (yawning, mood changes, neck stiffness before headache). Waiting for the headache to peak significantly reduces drug effectiveness because gastric stasis impairs absorption and central sensitization develops (allodynia). For triptans especially — take at headache onset, not during aura. Take an antiemetic 15-20 minutes before oral analgesics to improve gut absorption.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is medication overuse headache (MOH) and am I at risk?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: MOH (also called rebound headache) is a paradoxical worsening of headache caused by using acute headache medications too frequently — more than 10 days per month for triptans and opioids, or 15+ days for NSAIDs. The brain becomes dependent and headache occurs almost daily. It affects 1-2% of the general population and 30% of headache clinic patients. Warning signs: using medication more than 10-15 days/month, headache on waking, need for increasing medication doses. Treatment requires medically supervised withdrawal of the overused medication.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What preventive treatments are available for migraine?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Preventive (prophylactic) treatment is indicated when you have ≥4 migraine days per month or significant disability. Options include: Beta-blockers (propranolol, metoprolol) — first-line; Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline) — first-line especially with insomnia or depression; Antiepileptics (topiramate, valproate) — first-line; CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) — newest and most targeted; Botulinum toxin (Botox) — approved for chronic migraine; Evidence-based supplements (magnesium, riboflavin, CoQ10). Most preventives take 2-3 months for full effect.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Are triptans safe to take?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Triptans (sumatriptan, zolmitriptan, rizatriptan, eletriptan, etc.) are the gold standard acute treatment for moderate-severe migraine. They are safe for most people. However, they should NOT be used in people with: ischaemic heart disease, prior MI or stroke, uncontrolled hypertension, Prinzmetal angina, hemiplegic migraine, or during pregnancy. Triptan sensations (chest tightness, throat pressure — felt in ~15% of users) are mostly benign vasospasm effects, not cardiac events, but any chest pain should be assessed. Do not take more than 10 days per month to avoid MOH.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What are CGRP monoclonal antibodies for migraine?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: CGRP mAbs (erenumab/Aimovig, fremanezumab/Ajovy, galcanezumab/Emgality, eptinezumab/Vyepti) are the newest and most specific preventive treatments for migraine. They block CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide) — the central molecule driving migraine pain. Unlike older preventives, they were designed specifically for migraine. Given as monthly subcutaneous injections (or quarterly), they reduce migraine days by 50% in approximately 50% of patients, including those who have failed multiple other preventives. They are safe, well-tolerated, and have no CNS side effects.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I use migraine medications in pregnancy?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Migraine usually improves during the 2nd and 3rd trimesters. Safe acute treatments include: paracetamol (first-line, all trimesters) and metoclopramide for nausea. Ibuprofen is limited to 2nd trimester only. Triptans are generally avoided (limited safety data). Safe preventives include: magnesium supplements (strongly recommended), riboflavin 400mg, and CoQ10. Strictly AVOID: topiramate (teratogenic — cleft palate) and valproate (highly teratogenic — neural tube defects and cognitive impairment). Discuss all medications with your obstetrician and neurologist.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the 'FAST' mnemonic and why is it relevant to migraine?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: FAST stands for: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services — and is the stroke recognition tool. It is relevant to migraine because severe migraine headache can occasionally be confused with stroke. The critical distinction: migraine aura symptoms develop GRADUALLY over ≥5 minutes; stroke symptoms begin SUDDENLY and are maximal from onset. Any sudden ('thunderclap') onset of severe headache, sudden focal weakness, speech difficulty, or vision loss requires IMMEDIATE emergency services — do not assume it is migraine.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What dietary changes help with migraine?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Most important dietary measures: (1) Never skip meals — hypoglycaemia is a major trigger; (2) Stay well hydrated — 2-2.5 litres water daily; dehydration triggers attacks; (3) Limit or avoid alcohol, especially red wine; (4) Avoid tyramine-rich aged cheeses, processed meats, and MSG; (5) Reduce/eliminate caffeine or maintain a strictly consistent daily intake; (6) Eat plenty of magnesium-rich foods (spinach, pumpkin seeds, almonds, dark chocolate, legumes); (7) Consider magnesium 400-600mg daily supplement — Grade A clinical evidence. Keep a food diary for 4-6 weeks to identify your personal dietary triggers.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can stress cause migraines?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — stress is the most commonly reported migraine trigger (50-70% of migraineurs). Psychological stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, releasing cortisol and adrenaline that trigger the trigeminovascular cascade. The 'let-down' phenomenon is also very common: migraine attacks occurring on weekends or during holidays — when stress finally releases. Evidence-based stress management for migraine: CBT for headache (reduces frequency by 35-50%); biofeedback; mindfulness; regular yoga. These are Grade A recommendations in multiple migraine guidelines.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is migraine related to stroke?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Migraine with aura carries a small but real increased risk of ischaemic stroke — about 2-fold higher than the general population. The absolute risk is small but increases significantly with: being female, smoking, and using oestrogen-containing oral contraceptives (triple risk factor). Women with migraine with aura should ideally avoid combined oestrogen-containing contraceptives (progestogen-only pill is safer), not smoke, and control cardiovascular risk factors. Migrainous infarction (stroke during a migraine attack) is rare but possible.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is vestibular migraine?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Vestibular migraine is a migraine variant causing recurrent vertigo (spinning sensation or severe dizziness) lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours, combined with migraine symptoms (headache, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea). It is the second most common cause of recurrent spontaneous vertigo (after BPPV) affecting 1-3% of the population. It is frequently misdiagnosed as Ménière's disease. Treatment: migraine preventives (propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, venlafaxine) + vestibular rehabilitation physiotherapy.
